posts.quote: Abrego Garcia Self-Deported To Spain. His Lawyer Wants The Next President To Bring Him Back.
posts.alt: Photo of Kilmar Abrego Garcia in a white baseball cap and plaid shirt at a table during his April 2025 meeting with Sen. Chris Van Hollen in El Salvador, with a circle inset of DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin's official portrait. Text reads: Abrego Garcia Self-Deported To Spain. His Lawyer Wants The Next President To Bring Him Back. Break The Spin logo top left. Photo credits: Office of Sen. Chris Van Hollen; DHS.
posts.caption:
The Left's favorite "Maryland man" is gone.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia boarded a commercial flight out of the D.C. area and landed in Spain. DHS calls it what it is. Self-deportation.

"We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said.

Remember how this started. Sen. Chris Van Hollen flew to El Salvador to sit across a table from him. The media made him the face of the fight against Trump's deportations. Twenty months of headlines.

Now he's leaving. On a commercial flight. To a country he picked.

And his own lawyer is already planning the comeback.

His attorney, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, told NPR they "expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland." He called it "a temporary departure."

So this was never just about due process. It's about waiting out Trump.

Van Hollen is calling it a win. He says Abrego is "a free man" headed to "a country of his choice."

Now the honest part, because we don't do spin here. DHS calls him a "human trafficker, wife beater, gang member, and child predator." Those are accusations. He was never convicted of any of them. A federal judge in Tennessee threw out his human smuggling indictment in May as a vindictive prosecution. DOJ is appealing to bring it back.

But the bottom line doesn't change. A man who was here illegally is out of the country, and the people who turned him into a cause are already talking about bringing him back.
posts.first:
The facts: Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national, was arrested in Maryland in March 2025 and sent to El Salvador's CECOT prison in what an official later called an "administrative error." He was returned in June 2025 and indicted in Tennessee on human smuggling charges tied to a 2022 traffic stop. Judge Waverly Crenshaw dismissed that indictment May 22, 2026, finding a presumption of vindictive prosecution. DOJ has asked the Sixth Circuit to reinstate it. The administration tried to deport him to Liberia, and courts blocked it. He flew from the Washington area to Madrid Nov. 24 under an agreement worked out by his lawyers and government lawyers, The Washington Post reported.

Sources: DHS release (Nov. 24), AP, NPR, The Washington Post, ABC News, Reuters, WMAR (Van Hollen statement), Tennessee Star (DOJ appeal).

posts.theme: Trump gives Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom
posts.quote: They Disbarred Him Over 2020. Trump Just Gave Rudy Giuliani The Presidential Medal Of Freedom.
posts.alt: Photo from the White House of President Trump fastening the Presidential Medal of Freedom ribbon around Rudy Giuliani's neck in the Oval Office. Text reads: They Disbarred Him Over 2020. Trump Just Gave Rudy Giuliani The Presidential Medal Of Freedom. Break The Spin logo top left. Photo credit: The White House.
posts.caption:
They took his law license over 2020. Two states charged him. Both cases got dropped.

Now Rudy Giuliani has the Presidential Medal of Freedom, tied on by Trump himself in the Oval Office.

Giuliani says he is "honored and humbled."

9/11 mayor. Mob buster. Earned.
posts.first:
The facts: Awarded Nov. 24 in a private Oval Office ceremony. Giuliani was disbarred in New York and D.C.

Sources: White House, NBC News, ABC News, NY Post.

posts.theme: Huawei convicted in Brooklyn on 10 of 12 counts
posts.quote: Huawei Copied Cisco's Code And Swiped A T-Mobile Robot Part. Jury Verdict: Guilty On 10 Counts.
posts.alt: Photo of Huawei founder Ren Zhengfei in a close-up portrait, dark suit and red patterned tie, looking at the camera. Text reads: Huawei Copied Cisco's Code And Swiped A T-Mobile Robot Part. Jury Verdict: Guilty On 10 Counts. Break The Spin logo top left. Photo credit: Ren Zhengfei, Huawei founder, by cellanr, CC BY-SA 2.0.
posts.caption:
A Huawei employee walked into T-Mobile's lab, took a piece of their robot, put it in his backpack and walked out.

That's not a movie. That's from the Justice Department's case against Huawei. And a Brooklyn jury just convicted the Chinese tech giant on 10 of 12 federal counts.

Conspiracy to steal trade secrets. Bank fraud. Wire fraud. Money laundering conspiracy. Breaking U.S. sanctions on Iran.

Here's some of what DOJ says was proven at trial.

T-Mobile had a testing robot called "Tappy." Huawei signed a non-disclosure agreement "fully intending to violate the agreement." Employees sent photos and technical details back to China. When that wasn't enough, one of them carried a part out in his backpack.

Huawei copied the source code on Cisco routers, which DOJ called the "crown jewel" of Cisco technology. The engineers left Cisco's notes in the code and referred to Cisco by its name spelled backwards. "Ocsic."

A Huawei employee caught photographing Fujitsu equipment wore a badge saying he worked for "Weihua." Not Huawei. Weihua.

And for years Huawei lied to American banks about its business in Iran.

This is the company that wanted its equipment running inside American networks.

Now the honest part. A company can't go to prison. This ends in fines, forfeiture and restitution, and sentencing isn't until Sept. 14, 2027. The jury also acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge, racketeering conspiracy, and of conspiracy to obstruct justice. Huawei's lawyer called that a "profound rejection" of the government's case.

But guilty is guilty. Ten counts. An American jury looked at the evidence and said a Chinese tech giant stole from American companies and lied to American banks.

Remember that the next time someone tells you the China threat is overblown.
posts.first:
The facts: A federal jury in the Eastern District of New York convicted Huawei Technologies and three subsidiaries (Huawei Device, Futurewei Technologies and Huawei Device USA) on Nov. 24. Guilty counts include conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, IEEPA sanctions violations and money laundering conspiracy. Acquitted: racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice. Penalties are financial. Pictured: founder Ren Zhengfei, who was not a defendant.

Sources: U.S. Justice Department release (Nov. 24), AP, NBC News, The Guardian, Bloomberg Law.

posts.quote: Kim Gardner Disbarred 7-0. She Covered Her Own Ethics Fines With $5,004 Of Public Money.
posts.alt: Photo of the front entrance of the Supreme Court of Missouri building in Jefferson City, red brick with carved stone over wooden doors, with a circle inset of the Seal of the Supreme Court of Missouri. Text reads: Kim Gardner Disbarred 7-0. She Covered Her Own Ethics Fines With $5,004 Of Public Money. Break The Spin logo top left. Photo credit: Tony Webster, CC BY 2.0.
posts.caption:
Remember Kim Gardner? The St. Louis prosecutor who went after Gov. Eric Greitens?

She just lost her law license. 7-0.

Here's what she did. In 2022 the Missouri Supreme Court reprimanded her over the Greitens case and stuck her with $5,004.33 in fees and costs. She asked to pay it off in installments, like it was coming out of her own pocket.

Then she had her chief clerk cut her four checks from a public fund in her own office to pay herself back. She co-signed every one.

The court did not mince words: "she plainly intended to deceive this Court as to the source of the funds."

Her defense? Her lawyer said it was fine. The court noted that advice was an unsigned draft letter from an attorney who never reviewed the law on public funds.

This was the woman in charge of prosecuting crime in St. Louis. She resigned in 2023 under pressure. Now she can't practice law in Missouri at all.
posts.first:
The facts: In re Kimberly M. Gardner, No. SC101626, opinion by Judge Mary R. Russell, issued Nov. 24, 2026. The court found she violated Rules 4-8.4(b), (c) and (d) and rejected a hearing panel's recommendation of only a reprimand. She repaid the money and signed a federal pre-charge diversion agreement. She was never criminally charged.

Sources: Missouri Supreme Court opinion, Missouri Lawyers Media, Spectrum News, Just the News.

posts.theme: Trump: a pardon for Nvidia's Jensen Huang is "always an option"
posts.quote: Nvidia CEO Faces Congress Over A Suspected Chinese Spy. Trump: A Pardon Is "Always An Option."
posts.alt: Photo of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in close-up, gray hair and glasses, looking off to the side with a serious expression, taken at Stanford in April 2026. Text reads: Nvidia CEO Faces Congress Over A Suspected Chinese Spy. Trump: A Pardon Is "Always An Option." Break The Spin logo top left. Photo credit: Anderseidesvik, CC BY-SA 4.0.
posts.caption:
Nvidia's Jensen Huang is headed to Capitol Hill to answer questions about his relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly believed was a Chinese spy.

And the word "pardon" is already out there.

"It's always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary," Trump told the New York Post.

Trump also said, "I don't think he needs to take the Fifth," and "I want him to just tell the truth."

Huang hasn't been charged with anything. Attorney General Todd Blanche said he would have told the president if DOJ had information Huang was committing crimes.

But Republicans aren't waving this off. Sen. Kevin Cramer said with Huang back in charge, "the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens." Sen. John Kennedy expects him to take the Fifth anyway.

This man runs the company that makes the chips America's AI future runs on. China wants those chips badly.

Tell the truth, Jensen.
posts.first:
The facts: Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO after reports about the relationship, then was reinstated after Trump pushed Nvidia's board to bring him back. He has not been charged with any crime. He faces closed-door House interviews starting Dec. 1 and a public Senate Banking Committee hearing Dec. 3.

Sources: New York Post, NBC News, CNBC, The Guardian.
